newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S., Russian ministers seek START-2 ratification.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russian ministers seek START-2 ratification.

text.p: Defence leaders of the United States and Russia on Wednesday joined in pressing for ratification of the START-2 strategic nuclear arms reduction treaty by a reluctant and hostile Russian parliament.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said after talks with U.S. Defense Secretary William Perry that he favoured the treaty, already passed by the U.S. Senate, despite questions in Russia over its cost and NATO's enlargement into Eastern Europe.

Perry, who began a three-day visit to Russia on Wednesday, will on Thursday try to persuade deputies in the lower house of parliament to ratify START-2, which would slash strategic nuclear warheads to a third of Cold War levels.

"I not only favour it (START-2), I favour the next treaty, START-3, to continue the arms reduction," Rodionov told reporters after nearly three hours of discussions with Perry on bilateral and other military matters.
Rodionov refused to predict what the Duma would do, however, saying it depended on Perry's speech and the mood of lawmakers, most of whom currently appear opposed to the treaty.

Perry earlier told reporters travelling with him from Washington that a refusal to approve the treaty would cost Moscow and Washington billions of dollars each and would not delay NATO's expansion into eastern Europe.

"Reducing the number of weapons you have by half has to be a cost-saver," said Perry of the treaty, which would cut nuclear stockpiles on both sides to about 3,000 from their current levels of about 6,000.

He conceded the cuts were themselves expensive to carry out, but said savings from not having to maintain Cold War nuclear stockpiles were even greater. "The savings we estimate from the START treaty are measured in billions of dollars," Perry said.

The START-2 nuclear arms reduction treaty was signed in 1993. A senior U.S. defence official said privately on Wednesday that Perry and U.S. officials were confident the cuts could be completed by 2003, although some Russian officials were suggesting extending it to 2008.

Rodionov told reporters that he and Perry had discussed a wide range of ways to increase military ties between Moscow and Washington and had also covered subjects ranging from Bosnia to Russia's continuing objection to NATO expansion.
Perry said Rodionov would visit the United States for talks in December.
A senior U.S. defence official said the two had agreed to meet in Bosnia during the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday in late November and visit each other's peacekeeping troops there.

Republican U.S. Senator Richard Lugar of Indiana and Democratic Senator Joseph Lieberman of Connecticut, travelling with Perry, said Russian rejection of START-2 or a demand to amend the treaty would be a financial and military setback for both countries.

"Extending the time period (of START-2) does not save money, it simply extends the expense," said Lugar, who co-sponsored the Nunn-Lugar law which has provided $750 million to Russia since 1992 to help reduce weapons of mass destruction and prevent them from falling into the hands of terrorists.

Perry and the two senators will be joined by Democratic U.S. Senator Sam Nunn of Georgia on Friday to watch nuclear submarines being cut up at a Russian naval base near the Arctic Circle under the SALT-1 strategic arms reduction treay.

Rodionov faces a massive task in reforming Russia's struggling armed forces, which suffered humiliating military defeats in breakaway Chechnya, and in carrying out President Boris Yeltsin's promise to change Russia's military from a conscript force to a smaller, all-volunteer one.

"We have a lot of talk about reform in the armed forces. We have a lot of criticism that nothing is being done," Rodionov said. "All say that reform is necessary, but "not my service, don't touch my service'."
